newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Oil prices surge upward but market wary.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Oil prices surge upward but market wary.

text.p: World oil prices shot higher on Tuesday, but many traders remained wary of the sharp gains at a time of surging physical crude supply.

London futures for benchmark May Brent settled 75 cents higher at $20.25 a barrel having spent the morning in negative territory on the bearish effect of abundant supply in the Atlantic basin crude market.

Traders attributed the surge higher to a break above key technical resistance price levels by crude futures in New York which triggered buying by fund houses. "I think the market has been ready to push higher for sometime now," said one trader. "We might not hold onto these gains but at least its a sign the market may be bottoming."
Other market players were more cautious.
"I have no signals telling me to sell-off," said one dealer who trades on a technical analysis basis. "But I would like to see any moves higher done in heavier volume."
Longer term many physical traders were bearish, citing as one factor a 25-cent cut announced at the weekend in the price formula for sales of Iraq's Kirkuk crude in Europe.
The cut will mean Iraq will have to sell more oil to meet its cash target of $2 billion in earnings over six months under a U.N. oil-for-food deal.

Traders say that as long as Iraq has to operate under a revenue ceiling in a weak market, sales increases will have to chase falling prices in a vicious circle that will help drive the whole oil complex lower.
At current prices Iraq would have to export about 650,000 bpd to raise a billion dollars by June 9 in the second 90 days of the U.N. deal.
The Iraqi production increases could aggravate surging OPEC and non-OPEC production that together is poised to outstrip global demand in a sharp reversal of the situation in 1996.
"Prices are stuck in a zone of weakness from which there is no early escape," said a monthly oil report by British-based Centre for Global Energy Studies.
It added: "Prompt prices will have to remain below those for future deliveries to encourage companies to hold higher inventories."

By enabling companies to more than cover the cost of carrying extra stocks, sagging prompt prices should help the companies absorb 600,000 barrels per day of above-normal oil inventories this summer, it added.
But there was not much room for complacency, it said.
"Slightly higher non-OPEC output or slightly more output from OPEC than we have assumed would turn the expected oil price weakness into a collapse," it said.
